title: Index-based approaches
text: Index-based methods ask simple question: hunted site worse site hunted (lightly hunted)? measure thing places, example animal density hunting yield, compare . hunted site clearly lower, warning sign hunting may sustainable. methods popular need little data easy explain (Adounke et al. 2026; Weinbaum et al. 2013). main limit compare sites. tell exact level hunting things tip , difference two sites can causes hunting (soil, habitat, size forest patch). treat verdict signal look closer, final answer. package covers three indices: three take tidy data frame unquoted column names, three return small table sustainable column (TRUE FALSE). use bundled example data bushmeat_sites (density yield per transect) bushmeat_ages (one row per animal). made sake examples, real field data.
code: head(bushmeat_sites) #>   site_type transect density yield_kg effort_days #> 1 reference      T01      28       41          10 #> 2 reference      T02      31       44          11 #> 3 reference      T03      26       39           9 #> 4 reference      T04      33       45          10 #> 5 reference      T05      29       42          12 #> 6 reference      T06      30       43           9

title: Index-based approaches
text: compare animal density hunted site reference site. give one row per density estimate (example one row per transect), density column, column marks site, site reference. read output: hunted_value reference_value mean densities site. pct_change change hunted site relative reference, \[\text{pct\_change} = \frac{\text{hunted} - \text{reference}}{\text{reference}} \times 100.\] negative value means hunted site holds fewer animals. p_value comes one-sided t-test asking whether hunted site really lower (NA site fewer two replicates). sustainable FALSE hunted site significantly lower, TRUE otherwise.
code: ot_pdc(bushmeat_sites,        density = density,        group = site_type,        reference = "reference") #> <offtake: PDC (population density comparison)>  (index-based) #> Reference: Adounke et al. (2026); Weinbaum et al. (2013)  #>  #> # A tibble: 1 × 7 #>   hunted_site reference_site hunted_value reference_value pct_change     p_value #> * <chr>       <chr>                 <dbl>           <dbl>      <dbl>       <dbl> #> 1 hunted      reference              13.5            29.5      -54.2 0.000000150 #> # ℹ 1 more variable: sustainable <lgl>

title: Model-based approaches
text: Model-based methods work way round index-based ones. Instead comparing two sites, use biology species estimate many animals can taken year without shrinking population. compare estimate offtake actually observe. observed offtake larger estimate, hunting likely heavy (Adounke et al. 2026). function returns small table sustainable column TRUE observed harvest sits estimated safe level. use bundled example data duiker_demography (life-history values duikers) manu_settlements (hunting villages map). made examples.
code: duiker_demography #>                species density_k annual_take lifespan    b   a  w rmax #> 1          blue duiker        40         9.0       10 0.55 1.0 10 0.30 #> 2           red duiker        12         3.5       11 0.50 1.5 11 0.22 #> 3 yellow-backed duiker         3         0.8       12 0.45 2.0 12 0.15

title: Model-based approaches
text: common model bushmeat studies. safe harvest, called production \(P\), \[P = 0.6 \, K \, (\lambda_{\max} - 1) \, F.\] Reading piece piece: \(K\) density habitat can support (carrying capacity). \(0.6\,K\) density population grows fastest, produces surplus. \(\lambda_{\max}\) fastest yearly growth species can manage. part \((\lambda_{\max} - 1)\) surplus adds year. \(F\) safety fraction depends long animal lives: 0.6 short-lived species (5 years), 0.4 medium-lived (5 10 years) 0.2 long-lived species (10 years). Long-lived animals bounce back slowly, take smaller share. lambda_max, can let package work three life-history numbers using ot_lambda_max(): number female young per female per year (b), age first reproduction () age last reproduction (w). solves Cole’s (1954) equation, standard way turn basic life-history growth rate. Now model . pass life-history columns, lambda_max computed us, use lifespan set safety fraction F. production column estimated safe harvest, harvest observed, sustainable compares two.
code: ot_lambda_max(b = 0.55, a = 1, w = 10) #> [1] 1.542758 ot_pro(duiker_demography,        k = density_k,        harvest = annual_take,        b = b, a = a, w = w,        longevity = lifespan) #> <offtake: Pro (Robinson & Redford production model)>  (model-based) #> Reference: Robinson & Redford (1991)  #>  #> # A tibble: 3 × 5 #>   lambda_max     f production harvest sustainable #> *      <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>   <dbl> <lgl>       #> 1       1.54   0.4      5.21      9   FALSE       #> 2       1.41   0.2      0.590     3.5 FALSE       #> 3       1.32   0.2      0.117     0.8 FALSE

title: Model-based approaches
text: ot_pbr() comes marine mammal management deliberately cautious. safe removal \[\mathrm{PBR} = N_{\min} \times \tfrac{1}{2} R_{\max} \times F_R,\] \(N_{\min}\) low, cautious estimate population size (-count), \(R_{\max}\) maximum yearly growth rate, \(F_R\) recovery factor 0.1 1 lower want extra careful. give point estimate n coefficient variation cv, function works \(N_{\min}\) lower end plausible range.
code: ot_pbr(duiker_demography,        rmax = rmax,        removal = annual_take,        n = density_k,        fr = 0.5) #> <offtake: PBR (potential biological removal)>  (model-based) #> Reference: Wade (1998)  #>  #> # A tibble: 3 × 6 #>    nmin  rmax    fr   pbr removal sustainable #> * <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl> <lgl>       #> 1    40  0.3    0.5 3         9   FALSE       #> 2    12  0.22   0.5 0.66      3.5 FALSE       #> 3     3  0.15   0.5 0.112     0.8 FALSE

title: Model-based approaches
text: classic fisheries benchmark. assumes population follows logistic curve, growth fastest half carrying capacity slows population fills . largest steady catch can support \[\mathrm{MSY} = \frac{rK}{4},\] \(r\) growth rate \(K\) carrying capacity. also give current abundance n, function reports surplus abundance , sustainable yield right now rather ideal population size.
code: ot_msy(duiker_demography,        r = rmax,        k = density_k,        harvest = annual_take) #> <offtake: MSY (logistic maximum sustainable yield)>  (model-based) #> Reference: Schaefer (1954)  #>  #> # A tibble: 3 × 5 #>       r     k   msy harvest sustainable #> * <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl> <lgl>       #> 1  0.3     40 3         9   FALSE       #> 2  0.22    12 0.66      3.5 FALSE       #> 3  0.15     3 0.112     0.8 FALSE

title: Model-based approaches
text: Real environments steady. Good years bad years come go, variability eats much can safely take. ot_samse() follows idea, Manlik et al. (2022): projects population many times random good bad years, taking fixed number \(H\) year, \[N_{t+1} = \max\!\left(0,\; N_t\, e^{r_t} - H\right), \qquad r_t \sim \mathcal{N}(r_{\max}, \sigma_e),\] searches largest \(H\) still keeps population shrinking average. \(r_{\max}\) mean growth rate \(\sigma_e\) much swings year year. uses simulation, supply mean growth rate (rmax), much varies year year (sd_env), observed removal, starting population size. result usually bit lower formula without variability suggest, point. simplified version original method, built Vortex software includes biological detail. Use careful screen, cite Manlik et al. (2022) full approach.
code: # add a variability value and a starting size to the example data samse_data <- transform(duiker_demography,                         sd_env = 0.2,                         n0 = density_k)  ot_samse(samse_data,          rmax = rmax,          sd_env = sd_env,          removal = annual_take,          n0 = n0,          nsims = 200,          years = 40,          seed = 1) #> <offtake: SAMSE (sustainable anthropogenic mortality, stochastic)>  (model-based) #> Reference: Manlik et al. (2022)  #> Note: Simplified stochastic re-implementation of the SAMSE principle; not the original Vortex-based procedure.  #>  #> # A tibble: 3 × 6 #>      n0  rmax sd_env samse_limit removal sustainable #> * <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>       <dbl>   <dbl> <lgl>       #> 1    40  0.3     0.2      11.1       9   TRUE        #> 2    12  0.22    0.2       2.03      3.5 FALSE       #> 3     3  0.15    0.2       0.267     0.8 FALSE

title: Model-based approaches
text: models treat landscape one pot. practice hunting spread evenly: heavy near villages light far away. ot_biode(), Levi et al. (2009), captures . Near settlement animals get depleted (sink), remote areas stay full quietly resupply hunted zones (source). give location settlement many hunters live , plus parameters species hunting. model predicts animal density every point map, \[N(x, y) = \left[K^{\theta}\left(1 - \frac{e\,d\,h}{r}\sum_c P_c\,\varphi(\delta_c)\right)\right]_+^{1/\theta}, \qquad \varphi(\delta) = \frac{\exp\!\left(-\delta^2 / 2\sigma^2\right)}{2\pi\delta + 1}.\] words: settlement \(c\) presses animals around . pressure grows hunter population \(P_c\) fades distance \(\delta_c\) kernel \(\varphi\) (far hunters roam set \(\sigma\)). Add pressure settlements, population can still support whatever left carrying capacity \(K\). \([\,\cdot\,]_+\) just means density go zero. need handle hand; function across grid. summary reports, among things, frac_extirpated (share map pushed local extinction) mean_density. full predicted surface available ot_biode_surface(), ready mapping, catch per unit effort village can expect ot_biode_cpue(). ggplot2 installed, surface maps nicely raster, depletion halos around settlements.
code: res <- ot_biode(manu_settlements,                 x = x_km,                 y = y_km,                 humans = hunters,                 k = 25,                 r = 0.07,                 hphy = 40,                 kill_rate = 0.1,                 sigma = 6,                 resolution = 2) res #> <offtake: Biode (Levi et al. spatial source-sink model)>  (model-based) #> Reference: Levi et al. (2009)  #>  #> # A tibble: 1 × 7 #>   n_settlements mean_density min_density frac_extirpated frac_below_half_k #> *         <int>        <dbl>       <dbl>           <dbl>             <dbl> #> 1             4         19.5           0           0.118             0.193 #> # ℹ 2 more variables: cpue <dbl>, sustainable <lgl> head(ot_biode_surface(res)) #> # A tibble: 6 × 3 #>       x     y density #>   <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl> #> 1    -6     0    25.0 #> 2    -6     2    25.0 #> 3    -6     4    25.0 #> 4    -6     6    25.0 #> 5    -6     8    25.0 #> 6    -6    10    25.0 ot_biode_cpue(res) #> # A tibble: 4 × 5 #>   settlement     x     y humans local_cpue #>        <int> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>      <dbl> #> 1          1    12    20     60    0.00588 #> 2          2    40    35    110    0.00402 #> 3          3    55    18     90    0.00580 #> 4          4    28    48     45    0.00617 library(ggplot2)  surface <- ot_biode_surface(res)  ggplot(surface, aes(x, y, fill = density)) +   geom_raster() +   geom_point(data = manu_settlements,              aes(x_km, y_km), inherit.aes = FALSE,              colour = "white", shape = 4, size = 2) +   scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "density") +   coord_equal() +   labs(title = "Predicted game density", x = "km", y = "km") +   theme_minimal()

title: Age structure comparison (ASC) — ot_asc
text: Compares age/sex structure population hunted reference (unhunted lightly hunted) sites. Following Adounke et al. (2026), lower proportion juvenile class hunted site interpreted unsustainable (signal recruitment failure). Optionally full class--site frequency distribution can compared chi-squared test.

title: Age structure comparison (ASC) — ot_asc
code: ot_asc(   data,   stage,   group,   reference,   juvenile = NULL,   count = NULL,   method = c("proportion", "distribution"),   alpha = 0.05 )

title: Age structure comparison (ASC) — ot_asc
text: data data frame one row per sampled/harvested individual (one row per class count supplied). must contain age/sex class column (stage) site column (group). data already tallied, add count column pass count. stage <data-masked> Column giving age sex class individual (e.g. "juvenile"/"adult"). group <data-masked> Column identifying site / hunting treatment. reference Character scalar naming level group treated unhunted / lightly hunted reference. juvenile Character vector level(s) stage represent juvenile (pre-reproductive) class. Required method = "proportion". count <data-masked> Optional column counts, used data already aggregated class \(\times\) site. method "proportion" (default) compares juvenile proportion two sites two-sample test proportions; "distribution" compares whole class \(\times\) site table chi-squared test. alpha Significance level (default 0.05).

title: Age structure comparison (ASC) — ot_asc
text: offtake tibble one row per hunted site. Columns depend method. method = "proportion": hunted_site, reference_site two levels compared. juv_prop_hunted Proportion individuals juvenile class hunted site (0-1). juv_prop_reference Juvenile proportion reference site. pct_change Percentage change juvenile proportion relative reference; negative means fewer juveniles hunted site. p_value One-sided stats::prop.test() p-value lower juvenile proportion hunted site. sustainable FALSE juvenile share significantly lower hunted site. method = "distribution": hunted_site, reference_site two levels compared. statistic Pearson chi-squared statistic class \(\times\) site table. df Degrees freedom test. p_value Chi-squared p-value. sustainable FALSE two age structures differ significantly (p_value < alpha); interpret alongside direction shift (Weinbaum et al. 2013).

title: Biodemographic spatial source-sink model (Biode) — ot_biode
text: Predicts steady-state spatial distribution game density across landscape given location human population hunting settlements, following spatially explicit reaction-diffusion source-sink model Levi et al. (2009). Unlike non-spatial models (ot_pro(), ot_pbr(), ot_msy()), Biode maps hunting creates population sinks around settlements sources remote matrix.

title: Biodemographic spatial source-sink model (Biode) — ot_biode
code: ot_biode(   data,   x,   y,   humans,   k,   r,   hphy,   kill_rate,   sigma,   er = 0.02,   theta = 1,   resolution = 1,   margin = 3 * sigma,   extirpation_threshold = 1,   max_extirpated = 0.05 )

title: Biodemographic spatial source-sink model (Biode) — ot_biode
text: data data frame settlements, one row per settlement. Required columns: settlement coordinates (x, y) length unit sigma (e.g. kilometres), number hunters (humans). biological hunting parameters (k, r, hphy, kill_rate, sigma, ...) passed scalar arguments, columns, describe target species hunting technology, individual settlements. x, y <data-masked> Settlement coordinate columns, length unit sigma. humans <data-masked> Column giving number hunters (human population) settlement. k Carrying-capacity density K (individuals per cell area). r Intrinsic population growth rate. hphy Hunts per hunter per year (h). kill_rate Per-encounter kill probability d (weapon efficiency, 0-1). sigma Spatial spread hunting effort \(\sigma\) (mean hunting distance settlement), coordinate unit. er Coefficient converting game density encounter rate e (default 0.02, value used Levi et al. 2009). theta Density-dependence exponent \(\theta\) (default 1, logistic). resolution Grid cell size coordinate units (default 1). margin Landscape margin added around settlement bounding box, coordinate units (default 3 * sigma). extirpation_threshold Density cell counted locally extirpated (default 1). max_extirpated Maximum fraction landscape allowed extirpated assessment flagged sustainable (default 0.05).

title: Biodemographic spatial source-sink model (Biode) — ot_biode
text: one-row offtake tibble summarising landscape, columns: n_settlements Number settlements data. mean_density Mean predicted game density across grid cells. min_density Lowest predicted density (0 sink fully extirpated). frac_extirpated Fraction grid cells extirpation_threshold – share landscape locally wiped . frac_below_half_k Fraction cells density half carrying capacity k – broader depletion footprint. cpue Effort-weighted mean catch per unit effort predicted across landscape. sustainable Logical verdict: TRUE frac_extirpated <= max_extirpated. full predicted density surface per-settlement local CPUE attached attributes easily retrieved ot_biode_surface() ot_biode_cpue().

title: Biodemographic spatial source-sink model (Biode) — ot_biode
text: steady state model reduces closed form game density point landscape: $$N(x,y) = \Big[\,K^{\theta}\Big(1 - \frac{e\, d\, h}{r}\,        \sum_{c} P_c\, \varphi(\delta_c)\Big)\Big]_{+}^{1/\theta},$$ Gaussian hunting-effort kernel $$\varphi(\delta) = \frac{\exp\!\big(-\delta^2 / 2\sigma^2\big)}        {2\pi\,\delta + 1},$$ \(\delta_c\) distance point settlement c, P_c hunter population, K carrying capacity, r intrinsic growth rate, h (hphy) hunts per hunter per year, d (kill_rate) per-encounter kill probability (weapon efficiency), e (er) density--encounter coefficient, \(\theta\) density-dependence exponent, \([\cdot]_+\) denotes truncation zero. form taken directly Levi et al. (2009) published solver code.

what: Maximum finite rate of population increase (Cole's equation) — ot_lambda_max
title: Maximum finite rate of population increase (Cole's equation) — ot_lambda_max
text: Solves Cole's (1954) characteristic equation maximum intrinsic rate natural increase, returning finite (per-year) multiplication rate \(\lambda_{max} = e^{r_{max}}\). rate required production model ot_pro() supplied directly.

title: Maximum finite rate of population increase (Cole's equation) — ot_lambda_max
code: ot_lambda_max(b, a, w, interval = c(1e-06, 5))

title: Maximum finite rate of population increase (Cole's equation) — ot_lambda_max
text: b Mean annual number female offspring per female (.e. litter size \(\times\) litters per year \(\times\) proportion female). Age first reproduction (years). w Age last reproduction (years); often approximated lifespan. interval Search interval \(r_{max}\) passed stats::uniroot().

title: Maximum finite rate of population increase (Cole's equation) — ot_lambda_max
text: numeric vector, recycled length longest b, w, giving \(\lambda_{max}\) – maximum finite (per-year) rate increase. dimensionless greater 1 growing population (e.g. 1.30 means population can grow 30% per year). NA returned elements missing inputs positive root inside interval.

title: Maximum finite rate of population increase (Cole's equation) — ot_lambda_max
text: Cole's equation $$1 = e^{-r} + b\,e^{-r } - b\,e^{-r (w + 1)}$$ b mean annual number female offspring per female, age first reproduction w age last reproduction (years). equation solved numerically \(r\) \(\lambda_{max}=e^{r}\) returned.

title: Maximum finite rate of population increase (Cole's equation) — ot_lambda_max

what: Maximum sustainable yield of the logistic model (MSY) — ot_msy
title: Maximum sustainable yield of the logistic model (MSY) — ot_msy

title: Maximum sustainable yield of the logistic model (MSY) — ot_msy
code: ot_msy(data, r, k, harvest, n = NULL)

title: Maximum sustainable yield of the logistic model (MSY) — ot_msy
text: data data frame one row per population/stock. Required columns: intrinsic growth rate (r), carrying capacity (k) observed annual harvest (harvest); optionally current abundance (n). r <data-masked> Intrinsic rate natural increase (per year). k <data-masked> Carrying capacity K (population size density). harvest <data-masked> Observed annual harvest, basis k. n <data-masked> Optional current abundance, used compute surplus_at_n.

title: Maximum sustainable yield of the logistic model (MSY) — ot_msy
text: offtake tibble one row per input row columns: r Intrinsic growth rate used. k Carrying capacity used. msy Maximum sustainable yield, (r * k) / 4. harvest observed annual harvest, echoed back comparison. sustainable Logical verdict: TRUE harvest <= msy. surplus_at_n present n supplied: sustainable yield current abundance, (r * n) * (1 - n / k). Equals msy n = k / 2.

title: Maximum sustainable yield of the logistic model (MSY) — ot_msy
text: logistic model population growth $$\frac{dN}{dt} = r N \left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right)$$ whose surplus production maximised \(N = K/2\), giving $$MSY = \frac{rK}{4}.$$ harvest MSY considered unsustainable. current abundance n supplied, instantaneous surplus production abundance, \(rN(1 - N/K)\), also returned surplus_at_n, sustainable yield current (optimal) population size.

title: Potential biological removal (PBR) — ot_pbr
text: Estimates maximum number animals may removed population per year allowing reach stay near optimal size, compares observed human-caused removal. Originally developed marine mammal management (Wade 1998) increasingly applied terrestrial harvest (Adounke et al. 2026).

title: Potential biological removal (PBR) — ot_pbr
code: ot_pbr(   data,   rmax,   removal,   nmin = NULL,   n = NULL,   cv = NULL,   fr = 0.5,   percentile = 0.2 )

title: Potential biological removal (PBR) — ot_pbr
text: data data frame one row per population/stock. Required columns: maximum growth rate (rmax) observed annual removal (removal). must also supply population size, either minimum estimate (nmin) point estimate (n) optional coefficient variation (cv) nmin derived. rmax <data-masked> Maximum per-capita annual rate increase \(R_{max}\) (e.g. 0.04 many large mammals, 0.12 fast-breeding species). removal <data-masked> Observed annual human-caused removal (offtake), numbers animals. nmin <data-masked> Minimum population estimate. Optional n (optionally cv) supplied. n <data-masked> Point abundance estimate, used cv derive nmin. cv <data-masked> Coefficient variation n (e.g. 0.3 30% CV). Treated 0 (nmin = n) omitted. fr Recovery factor \(F_R\) [0.1, 1] (default 0.5). May single value embraced column. percentile Lower percentile used convert n/cv nmin (default 0.20, giving z = 0.842).

title: Potential biological removal (PBR) — ot_pbr
text: offtake tibble one row per input row columns: nmin Minimum population estimate used (supplied, derived n cv). rmax Maximum per-capita rate increase used. fr Recovery factor applied. pbr Potential biological removal – maximum sustainable annual removal, numbers animals. removal observed annual removal, echoed back comparison. sustainable Logical verdict: TRUE removal <= pbr, FALSE observed removal exceeds PBR.

title: Potential biological removal (PBR) — ot_pbr
text: $$PBR = N_{min}\; \tfrac{1}{2} R_{max}\; F_R$$ N_min conservative (minimum) population estimate, \(R_{max}\) maximum per-capita annual rate increase \(F_R\) recovery factor 0.1 1. removal exceeding PBR indicates unsustainability. N_min may supplied directly nmin, computed abundance estimate n coefficient variation cv lower tail log-normal distribution, \(N_{min} = N / \exp\!\big(z\sqrt{\ln(1+CV^2)}\big)\), z standard-normal quantile chosen percentile (z = 0.842 20th percentile, recommended Wade 1998).

title: Potential biological removal (PBR) — ot_pbr
text: Wade, P. R. (1998) Calculating limits allowable human-caused mortality cetaceans pinnipeds. Marine Mammal Science 14, 1-37. doi:10.1111/j.1748-7692.1998.tb00688.x

title: Robinson & Redford production model (Pro) — ot_pro
text: Estimates maximum sustainable harvest (production) population carrying capacity, maximum rate increase longevity-based mortality factor, compares observed annual offtake. widely used model bushmeat sustainability assessments (Adounke et al. 2026).

title: Robinson & Redford production model (Pro) — ot_pro
code: ot_pro(   data,   k,   harvest,   lambda = NULL,   f = NULL,   longevity = NULL,   b = NULL,   a = NULL,   w = NULL )

title: Robinson & Redford production model (Pro) — ot_pro
text: data data frame one row per species population unit. Required columns: carrying capacity (k) observed annual offtake (harvest), basis (per km^2, absolute counts). must also supply growth rate – either lambda column life-history columns b, , w – mortality factor – either f column longevity column. k <data-masked> Carrying capacity K (density per km^2, absolute population size). harvest <data-masked> Observed annual offtake, basis k. lambda <data-masked> Maximum finite rate increase \(\lambda_{max}\) (dimensionless, > 1). Optional b, , w given. f <data-masked> Mortality factor F (0.2, 0.4 0.6). Optional longevity given. longevity <data-masked> Age last reproduction / lifespan (years), used derive F f given. b, , w <data-masked> Life-history columns passed ot_lambda_max() lambda given: annual female offspring per female (b), age first reproduction () age last reproduction (w), years.

title: Robinson & Redford production model (Pro) — ot_pro
text: offtake tibble one row per input row columns: lambda_max Maximum finite rate increase used, whether supplied computed b, , w. f Mortality factor F used (0.2, 0.4 0.6). production Estimated maximum sustainable harvest P, basis k harvest (e.g. individuals per km^2 per year). harvest observed annual offtake, echoed back comparison. sustainable Logical verdict: TRUE harvest <= production, FALSE observed offtake exceeds estimated production.

title: Robinson & Redford production model (Pro) — ot_pro
text: production (maximum sustainable number can taken per year) $$P = 0.6\,K\,(\lambda_{max} - 1)\,F$$ K carrying-capacity density (population size), \(\lambda_{max}\) maximum finite rate increase F mortality factor set longevity: F = 0.6 short-lived species (lifespan ~ 5 years), 0.4 medium-lived (5-10 years) 0.2 long-lived species (> 10 years) (Robinson & Redford 1991). factor 0.6 K density production assumed maximal. observed harvest exceeds P harvest considered unsustainable. Supply \(\lambda_{max}\) lambda directly, leave NULL provide life-history columns b, , w computed ot_lambda_max() (Cole's equation). Provide mortality factor either f directly longevity column.

title: Robinson & Redford production model (Pro) — ot_pro

Required columns: mean maximum growth rate (rmax), environmental standard deviation (sd_env), observed annual removal (removal) starting population size (n0). rmax <data-masked> Mean maximum annual growth rate \(r_{max}\) log scale (\(\lambda = e^{r_{max}}\); e.g. 0.10 ~10% growth). sd_env <data-masked> Environmental standard deviation annual growth rate \(\sigma_e\) (larger = year--year variability, lower sustainable removal). removal <data-masked> Observed annual human-caused removal (animals per year). n0 <data-masked> Starting (ideally minimum, N_min-style) population size. years Projection horizon years (default 50). nsims Number Monte-Carlo trajectories per candidate removal (default 500). tol Convergence tolerance bisection, fraction n0 (default 0.001). seed Optional integer seed reproducibility (uses common random numbers across candidate removals).

Use precautionary screening tool cite Manlik et al. (2022) concept. projection stochastic exponential model constant annual take H: $$N_{t+1} = \max\!\big(0,\; N_t\, e^{r_t} - H\big), \quad       r_t \sim \mathrm{Normal}(r_{max},\, \sigma_e).$$ stochastic growth rate \(\rho(H) = \mathrm{mean}\, \log(N_{t}/N_{0})/T\). SAMSE limit largest H \(\rho(H) \ge 0\), found bisection. observed removal SAMSE limit indicates unsustainability.

code: # One row per stock. Columns: #   rmax = mean max growth rate (log scale, per year) #   sd = environmental SD of the annual growth rate #   n0 = starting population size #   take = observed annual removal (animals) d <- data.frame(stock = "A", rmax = 0.10, sd = 0.25, n0 = 500, take = 20) ot_samse(d, rmax = rmax, sd_env = sd, removal = take, n0 = n0,          nsims = 200, years = 40, seed = 1) #> <offtake: SAMSE (sustainable anthropogenic mortality, stochastic)>  (model-based) #> Reference: Manlik et al.
